 Seniors Get a $900 Social Security Raise in 2027. Inflation Could Take $1,039
 By Rich Duprey 
 Published November 12, 2026, 12:21pm ET · 3 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A 3.6% COLA lifts the average Social Security check about $900 in 2027, but it reflects price changes through September 2026, not next year's bills.
 Higher Medicare Part B premiums shrink the raise to roughly $821, and a retiree facing 4% essential-cost inflation falls about $139 short.
 Retirees should budget around their net deposit and track personal inflation, since savings withdrawals covering shortfalls can raise taxes on Social Security benefits.

 In January, the average retired worker’s Social Security check rises from $2,095 to $2,170 a month. That $900 annual bump comes from the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA , set for 2027.
 For someone living mostly on that check, $900 feels like breathing room. Whether it actually is depends on changes in groceries, electricity, rent and doctor bills next year. Older adults were already skeptical before this round: research conducted by AARP in September 2025 found they felt the previous raise fell short of rising prices.
 Your 2027 Raise Is Built on Last Year’s Prices
 The COLA comes from an inflation measure called the CPI-W, which tracks prices paid by urban wage earners and clerical workers. Social Security compares the average for July through September with the same three months a year earlier. So your 2027 raise reflects price changes that already happened through September 2026. It can’t account for what your bills do next year.
 The second wrinkle is whose spending gets measured. The government keeps a separate research index for Americans 62 and older that gives more weight to housing and medical care. No benefit is tied to it. If rent, utilities and health care eat most of your budget, your personal inflation rate can run ahead of the number that sets your raise.
 Medicare Takes the First Bite Before You See a Dime
 Most retirees have their Medicare Part B premium deducted straight from their Social Security check. The standard premium is $202.90 a month in 2026. Medicare’s trustees estimate it will rise to $209.50 in 2027, though that figure isn’t final yet.
 If the estimate holds, that’s $79.20 more a year in premiums. Your $900 raise drops to about $821 before you’ve bought a single grocery cart.
 Napkin Math Shows Where the $1,039 Comes From
 Picture a single retiree spending $2,000 a month on necessities like food, electricity, housing and out-of-pocket medical costs. If those expenses rise 4% in 2027, that adds $960 over the year.
 Add the Medicare increase and the new costs total roughly $1,039. That’s about $139 more than the raise. This household ends 2027 with less spending money than it had in 2026, despite a bigger check.
 For this budget, the raise keeps pace only if essential costs climb less than about 3.4%. For context, overall consumer prices rose roughly 3.7% from September 2025 to September 2026, so a 4% year for necessities is a reasonable stress test. Your own numbers will differ. A retiree who owns a paid-off home and spends less on utilities may come out ahead.
 How the Gap Connects to Savings and Future Raises
 For retirees with an IRA or 401(k), a shortfall like $139 usually gets covered by slightly larger withdrawals. That’s manageable once. The risk is simply doing it every year without noticing, because money pulled from a traditional IRA is taxable and can pull more of your Social Security into taxable income .
 There’s a reassuring side to the lag. If prices run hot through 2027, that inflation shows up in the 2028 COLA, which builds on your new, higher base. Social Security tends to catch up, just a year late. Your savings act as the bridge in between.
 Two Moves to Make Before January
 Check your net deposit. Social Security mails a notice showing your new benefit and Medicare premium. The amount that lands in your bank account is the number to budget around. Treating the full $900 as available is the easiest mistake to make and the hardest to undo once it’s tied up in new monthly commitments.
 Measure your own inflation rate. Pull last year’s bills for your four biggest categories, usually housing, food, utilities and health care, and compare them with this year’s. If your costs are climbing faster than 3.6%, you’ll know early that savings may need to fill a gap, and you can plan the withdrawal rather than react to it.
